# 2 Samuel Chapter 1 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 168v–169r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_001_page_001.jpg, 2SA_001_page_002.jpg

---

**1** And it came to pass after the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking the Amalekites, that David stayed in Ziklag two days.

**2** And on the third day, behold, a man came from the camp, from Saul, with his garments torn and earth upon his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed down.

**3** And David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."

**4** And David said to him, "How did things go? Tell me, please." And he said, "The people fled from the battle, and many of the people also fell and died, and Saul and Jonathan his son also died."

**5** And David said to the young man who brought him word, "How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?"

**6** And the young man who brought him word said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and behold, Saul was leaning upon his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were pressing hard upon him.

**7** And he turned behind him and saw me, and he called to me. And I said, 'Here I am.'

**8** And he said to me, 'Who are you?' And I said to him, 'I am an Amalekite.'

**9** And he said to me, 'Stand over me and put me to death, for anguish has seized me, yet my life is still wholly in me.'

**10** So I stood over him and put him to death, for I knew that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."

**11** Then David took hold of his garments and tore them, and so also did all the men who were with him.

**12** And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

**13** And David said to the young man who had brought him word, "Where are you from?" And he said, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite."

**14** And David said to him, "How is it that you were not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the anointed of the LORD?"

**15** Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go near and strike him down." And he struck him, and he died.

**16** And David said to him, "Your blood be upon your own head, for your own mouth testified against you, saying, 'I put to death the anointed of the LORD.'"

**17** And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son.

**18** And he said it should be taught to the sons of Judah — "The Bow." Behold, it is written in the Book of the Upright:

**19** "The glory of Israel is slain upon your heights!
How the mighty have fallen!

**20** Tell it not in Gath,
proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon,
lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice,
lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.

**21** O mountains of Gilboa,
let there be no dew and no rain upon you, nor fields of offerings!
For there the shield of the mighty was defiled,
the shield of Saul — no longer anointed with oil.

**22** From the blood of the slain,
from the fat of the mighty,
the bow of Jonathan did not turn back,
and the sword of Saul did not return empty.

**23** Saul and Jonathan —
beloved and pleasant in their lives,
and in their death they were not divided.
They were swifter than eagles,
they were stronger than lions.

**24** O daughters of Israel, weep over Saul,
who clothed you in scarlet with luxury,
who set ornaments of gold upon your garments.

**25** How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle!
Jonathan lies slain upon your heights!

**26** I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan.
Very pleasant were you to me.
Your love to me was wonderful,
surpassing the love of women.

**27** How the mighty have fallen,
and the weapons of war have perished!"

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verse 9 — "anguish":** The Hebrew *shavats* is a rare term suggesting convulsive agony or cramping. I render "anguish" to preserve the dignity of the formal register while acknowledging the physical torment described.

**Verse 18 — "The Bow":** The lament is given the title *Qeshet* ("The Bow"), possibly referring to Jonathan's famed weapon (cf. v.22). The reference to the Book of the Upright (*Sefer ha-Yashar*) indicates this was preserved in an ancient collection of poems, now lost, also referenced in Joshua 10:13.

**Verse 19 — "The glory":** Hebrew *ha-tsevi* can mean "the beauty," "the glory," or "the gazelle." In the formal register, "the glory" captures the sense of national honor and splendor that has been struck down, while allowing the animal imagery to remain subtextual.

**Verse 21 — "fields of offerings":** The phrase *sedey terumot* remains one of the most debated in the lament. I render literally as "fields of offerings" following the Masoretic vowel pointing, though many scholars emend to "fields that surge upward" (i.e., fertile uplands). The curse denies the mountains both heavenly moisture and earthly fertility.

**Verse 26 — "surpassing the love of women":** The Hebrew *nifle'atah* (was wonderful) and the comparison use the standard vocabulary of covenantal intimacy. The formal translation preserves the text as written without interpretive expansion. The bond described is that of a covenant-brother, consistent with the *berit* (covenant) established in 1 Samuel 18:3.

**Consistent terms:** Saul (Sha'ul), Jonathan (Yehonatan), the LORD (YHWH), anointed (mashiach), mighty/mighty ones (gibborim).

*— LOGOS*
